proposal.title: NoteProof: Bitcoin timestamps and an AI-tagged knowledge graph for students' lecture notes

proposal.problem: Students in our department share their lecture notes with each other, but the notes end up scattered across WhatsApp groups, photographed pages and a few Drive folders. In a survey of 20 third- and fourth-year students on 16 October 2026, 17 said they share their own notes, 3 of them regularly; 10 of the 17 share them in WhatsApp groups and 9 send photos of the pages. Five of the 20 said a note of theirs had been passed on or sold without their name or permission, and 5 more could not tell, because nobody can follow a note once it is shared. Nobody can prove who had a note first either: file dates change whenever a file is copied, and the owner of a shared folder can edit or replace anything in it. Before an exam, the median student needs 10 to 20 minutes to find a note on one topic, and 13 of the 20 need 10 minutes or more, scrolling through chats with no way to tell which copy is the original. Authors get no credit for their work and readers study from whatever copy they find; 14 of the 20 said they would use an archive that finds notes by course and topic and proves whose note each one is.
proposal.mission: Give every Note author a way to register a lecture note and receive a proof, anchored on the Bitcoin signet in the way Nakamoto's timestamp server describes, that the note existed in their hands on that day; let an AI tagger file each note under a shared course and topic vocabulary; and let every Note reader find notes by topic, see who registered each one first, and be warned about copies of earlier notes.
proposal.outcome: A student uploads a note after class, confirms the course and topics the AI suggests, and the next day holds a proof linked to a Bitcoin transaction; before the exam a classmate searches a topic, finds that note with its author and date, and anyone can check the proof without trusting the archive or the people who run it.

entities.def: a student's own lecture note file (PDF, photo or text), a schema:CreativeWork identified by its SHA-256 hash
a PROV-O activity recording which student account registered which note hash, and when
a SKOS concept for a course topic, such as 'Transaction fees' under SEN0401, with broader and narrower topics
a signet transaction whose OP_RETURN output holds the Merkle root of one day's note hashes
a note's Merkle path and the txid, which anyone can check against the block

proposal.techWhy: Each note is described as a schema.org CreativeWork, and PROV-O records the registration activity: which student account registered which hash, and when, so the archive's history is standard linked data that the proof page can show. A SKOS concept scheme holds the courses and their topics, starting from SEN0401's fourteen chapters, with broader and narrower links; the AI tagger may only choose concepts from it, and a SPARQL property path over skos:narrower lets a search for 'Transactions' also find notes on 'Transaction fees'. SHACL shapes, run with pySHACL, refuse a note without a course, an unknown topic or an unconfirmed tag. Records travel as JSON-LD, RDFLib handles them in Python and Oxigraph stores them. Search answers follow the GraphRAG pattern: the model only phrases notes the graph returns and cites them. Stable IRIs give every proof a permanent link, and the KVKK regime decides that only hashes reach the chain.

proposal.spec: The system lets a student upload a lecture note as a PDF, a photo or text. It computes the note's SHA-256 hash and records the registration with PROV-O. An AI tagger reads the note's text and suggests a course, topics from the SKOS vocabulary and a two-sentence summary; nothing is saved until the author confirms, and the SHACL shapes refuse a note without a course or with an unknown topic. A copy check compares the new note with earlier notes and links possible copies to the earlier note's proof. Once a day the timestamp service builds a Merkle tree of the day's hashes and writes its root in an OP_RETURN output of a Bitcoin signet transaction, giving each note a Merkle path. Readers search by course and topic, including narrower topics. A public proof page recomputes a note's hash, walks its Merkle path and shows the block time, without needing the archive's server.

scenarios.text: Given a note registered and confirmed today, when the daily timestamp has one confirmation, then the note's proof page shows its hash, its Merkle path, the signet txid and the block time
Given a note file that was changed by one character after it was timestamped, when its proof is checked, then the hash does not match and the page says it is not the registered file
Given a note whose author picks a topic that is not in the vocabulary, when the author confirms it, then the note is refused and the author is asked to choose a topic from the list

proposal.activity:
Swimlanes: Note author · NoteProof services · Bitcoin signet · Note reader or verifier

A. Register a note
1. Start: the note author uploads a note (PDF, photo or text).
2. The registration service checks the file type and size. [not allowed] → the upload is refused with the reason → end.
3. It computes the note's SHA-256 hash. [hash already registered] → the page shows the earlier registration and its proof → end.
4. Fork, in parallel:
   4a. The AI tagger extracts the text and suggests a course, topics from the SKOS vocabulary and a two-sentence summary.
   4b. The copy checker compares the text with earlier notes.
5. Join: the author sees the suggestions and any similar earlier note.
6. The author confirms or corrects every tag. [author cancels] → nothing is saved → end.
7. pySHACL validates the confirmed tags against the shapes. [invalid] → the violations are shown and the author returns to step 6.
8. [similar earlier note found] → the note is marked as a possible copy and linked to the earlier note's proof.
9. The note and its PROV-O registration are stored and its hash is queued; the author sees "proof pending". End of the author's flow.

B. Daily timestamp (time event: every day at 23:00)
10. The timestamp service collects the day's queued hashes. [queue empty] → end.
11. It builds the Merkle tree and puts the 32-byte root in an OP_RETURN output.
12. It broadcasts the transaction to the Bitcoin signet through Bitcoin Core and waits for one confirmation. [not confirmed within 6 blocks] → it bumps the fee and broadcasts again.
13. It stores the txid, the block height and each note's Merkle path, and marks the notes "timestamped". End.

C. Find and check a note
14. The reader searches by course and topic; the search also covers narrower topics.
15. The reader opens a note card with its author, date and proof badge.
16. On the proof page the browser recomputes the file's hash, walks its Merkle path and fetches the block from a public signet node.
17. [hash and root match] → "proven", with the block time. [no match] → "not the registered file". End.
proposal.sequence: The upload page sends the file to the registration service, which computes the SHA-256 hash, extracts the text and asks the tagger and the copy checker in parallel. The tagger asks the language model for concepts limited to the SKOS vocabulary and returns them; the copy checker compares the text's embedding with earlier notes and returns any match. The author confirms; the service asks pySHACL to validate and stores the note and its PROV-O registration in Oxigraph. Each night the timestamp service reads the day's hashes, builds the Merkle tree, asks the Bitcoin Core signet node to fund and broadcast an OP_RETURN transaction, waits for a confirmation and stores the txid and each Merkle path. The proof page recomputes the hash in the browser, walks the path and asks a public signet node for the block.

proposal.classModel: Note is a schema:CreativeWork identified by its SHA-256 hash, with a title, a file type, a summary, one Course and one or more Topics. Course and Topic are skos:Concepts in one scheme, linked by skos:broader and skos:narrower. Registration is a prov:Activity that generated the Note's record, associated with a StudentAccount (pseudonymous) at a time. A new version of a note is a new Note linked by prov:wasRevisionOf. DailyTimestamp holds a date, a Merkle root, a signet txid and a block height; every Note has one Proof, its Merkle path, pointing to a DailyTimestamp. CopyWarning links a Note to an earlier Note with a similarity score.

proposal.model_Data: Design-level class diagram: Note (schema:CreativeWork), Course and Topic (skos:Concept), Registration (prov:Activity), StudentAccount (prov:Agent, pseudonymous), DailyTimestamp, Proof and CopyWarning; NoteShape requires a hash, a course and at least one topic from the scheme, and no class holds a real name or student number.
proposal.model_Security: State machine of a note: uploaded, tagged, confirmed, registered, timestamped, superseded. Only the author moves a note from tagged to confirmed; only confirmed notes are queued for the daily timestamp; a timestamped note is never edited - a new version is a new note that revises it; a file whose hash does not match its proof is shown as not the registered file.
proposal.model_Interaction: Sequence: the author uploads a note; the page shows the AI's suggested course, topics and summary; the author confirms or changes each one from the vocabulary list; the page sends the confirmed tags; the service validates them and returns the registration time and the note's pending proof.
proposal.model_User_interface: Storyboard: an upload page with a drop area and the AI's suggestions as removable chips; a search page with course and topic filters and note cards showing author, date and a proof badge (pending, proven or altered); a proof page with the hash, the Merkle path drawn as a small tree, the txid and the block time; Turkish labels, phone first.
proposal.model_Architecture: Component diagram: RegistrationService (hashing, PROV-O, pySHACL) writing to Oxigraph; Tagger, the only component that calls the language model for tags, limited to the SKOS concepts; CopyChecker comparing text embeddings; TimestampService holding the signet wallet key and talking to a Bitcoin Core node; SearchService answering SPARQL; ProofPage verifying in the browser.
proposal.model_Interface: Component boundary: the proof is a small JSON-LD file with the note's hash, its Merkle path, the txid and the block height; the ProofPage needs only this file, the note file and any public signet node, so it works when the archive's server is gone; the registration API returns the named shape violations.
proposal.chainDesign: The project is a direct implementation of the timestamp server in section 3 of Nakamoto's Bitcoin paper: hash the items, publish the hash widely, and the publication proves the items existed at that time; each new block includes the previous one, so every later block reinforces the timestamp. We use the Bitcoin signet through a Bitcoin Core node and its RPC interface, with regtest for automated tests. Each note is hashed with SHA-256; once a day the hashes form a Merkle tree (section 7 of the paper, from Bayer, Haber and Stornetta) and one transaction spends a UTXO into an OP_RETURN output carrying the 32-byte root, so any number of notes costs one transaction. A note's proof is its Merkle path and the txid; checking it is like simplified payment verification (section 8): the verifier needs the path and the block, not a full node. A blockchain is needed because the archive and whoever runs it can change dates in their own database; only a public record that nobody can rewrite without redoing the proof-of-work of that block and every block after it gives a time that no single party controls. Only the root goes on chain, never note content or personal data.
